description: We’re a three-person team (Rahul, Ashok and Mrinalini) building a data-driven answer to the question “Where on Earth should we rehearse for the Moon and Mars?” We work as a tight, fast team. Everyone pairs with AI coding assistants so we can ship a full pipeline, backend and map in one weekend.
summary: Analog Earth is a data-driven tool that finds the places on Earth most like the Moon’s south pole or Jezero crater on Mars. Today’s analog test sites were mostly chosen by expert judgement; we search the whole planet instead. We measure the same terrain and climate features (relief, slope, roughness at several scales, temperature, dryness) on Earth, the Moon and Mars using open NASA elevation data (LOLA, MOLA) alongside global Earth datasets, then score all 8.7 million land cells of a 5 km global grid against each target. An interactive 3D globe shows the top sites, explains each match feature by feature in real units, and can hide the famous analogs to reveal overlooked ones, such as the Peruvian Andes for the lunar pole and Egypt’s Eastern Desert for Jezero. Every site also states what does not match and what Earth can never replicate: gravity, vacuum and radiation. This gives mission planners a transparent, repeatable way to choose where to test rovers, instruments and crews.
details:
What it does and how it works
Analog Earth ranks every place on Earth by how closely it resembles a lunar or Martian target: the Moon’s south polar cap (poleward of 85°S) or a 150 km disc around Jezero crater. We compute the same features on all three bodies: relief, slope, roughness at 5, 10 and 20 km, how roughness changes with scale, temperature and dryness. Each feature is measured in kilometre-sized windows so datasets with different resolutions stay comparable. All 8.7 million land cells of a 0.05° (about 5 km) global grid are then compared with the target, both in real units and by rank on Earth’s own distribution. Priority presets (balanced, rover mobility, cold-trap and ice, thermal cycling) weight the result. An interactive 3D globe shows the top sites, a per-feature breakdown for each one, and a chart comparing the site with its target.

Benefits and intended impact
Analog sites are mostly chosen by expert judgement. Analog Earth gives mission planners and researchers a transparent, repeatable way to shortlist places for testing rovers, instruments and crew procedures, and to see exactly what each site is and is not good for. It surfaces candidates outside the usual list, such as the Peruvian Andes for the lunar pole (relief 1749 m vs 1789 m) and Egypt’s Eastern Desert for Jezero (slope 1.44° vs 1.47°, 6 mm of rain a year). Known analogs score well without being tuned for: Atacama reaches 0.85 for Jezero.

Tools and data
Python 3.11 with xarray, rasterio, NumPy and FastAPI for the pipeline and API; MapLibre GL JS and Plotly for the globe app; 122 automated tests. Data: NASA LOLA lunar elevation and permanently shadowed regions, NASA MOLA Mars topography, NOAA ETOPO 2022 Earth relief and WorldClim 2.1 climate. Everything runs in about 15 minutes on an 8 GB laptop.

How it is creative
Instead of studying one site, we score the whole planet and let the data nominate sites. A “hide famous” switch removes the well-known analogs to reveal overlooked ones. Every result shows its mismatches next to its matches, and results we consider misleading (for example, a rainforest that wins on terrain alone) are shown as warnings rather than hidden.

Factors we considered
Honesty about limits came first: Earth cannot replicate reduced gravity, vacuum or the thin Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environment, and every site says so. Features the source data cannot resolve are left out, never guessed. Temperature is weak evidence in this build (Earth data is air temperature, and Mars temperature is not scored), and there is no mineral or ice map, so ice-sheet sites carry a flag. Scores are relative to Earth’s land and are not comparable between the Moon and Mars. Next steps are NASA surface temperature and rainfall (MODIS, GPM IMERG) and mineral maps (EMIT, ASTER).
